title: Patrick Stewart
wiki_lead:
Sir Patrick Stewart (13 July 1940 – 28 October 2026) was an English actor. With a career spanning over 60 years on stage and screen, he received numerous accolades, including three Laurence Olivier Awards and a Grammy Award, as well as nominations for a Tony Award, three Golden Globe Awards, four Emmy Awards, and three Screen Actors Guild Awards. He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for his services to drama in 2010.
Stewart became a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) in 1966 and later acted in several productions with the Royal National Theatre. On the West End stage, he earned two Laurence Olivier Awards for Best Actor in a Supporting Role for playing Enobarbus in Antony and Cleopatra (1979) and King Claudius in Hamlet (2009). He made his Broadway debut in A Midsummer Night's Dream (1971). He later played the title role in Macbeth (2008), earning a nomination for the Tony Award for Best Actor in a Play. Stewart also acted alongside Ian McKellen in multiple plays, including repertory productions of Waiting for Godot and No Man's Land, which they performed on the West End and on Broadway.
He gained international stardom for his portrayal of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the sci-fi series Star Trek: The Next Generation (1987–1994), a role he reprised in a series of four films (1994–2002) and Star Trek: Picard (2020–2023). He acted in the television projects Fall of Eagles (1974); I, Claudius (1976); Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy (1979); Moby Dick (1998); A Christmas Carol (1999); and The Lion in Winter (2003). He also took guest roles in the sitcoms Frasier (2003) and Extras (2005) and collaborated with Seth MacFarlane, voicing CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock in the animated sitcom American Dad! (2005–2026), narrating the two Ted films (2012, 2015), and starring in the Starz sitcom Blunt Talk (2015–2016).
In film, Stewart gained further stardom portraying Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film series (2000–2017), reprising the role in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (2022–2026), with Avengers: Doomsday being his final film performance. He also acted in Hedda (1975), Excalibur (1981), Dune (1984), Robin Hood: Men in Tights (1993), Jeffrey (1995), Match (2014), Green Room (2015), and The Kid Who Would Be King (2019), with voice roles in The Pagemaster (1994), The Prince of Egypt (1998), Jimmy Neutron: Boy Genius (2001), and The Sheep Detectives (2026).

Early life and education
Patrick Stewart was born on 13 July 1940 in Mirfield, then in the West Riding of Yorkshire, to Gladys (née Barrowclough), a weaver and textile worker, and Alfred Stewart, who served in the British Army during the Second World War, and took part in the Dunkirk evacuation. Alfred as a result suffered from combat fatigue, later known as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). He later became a regimental sergeant major in the 2nd Parachute Brigade seeing service in the south of France and Greece. After the war Alfred worked as a general labourer and postman. Patrick had two older brothers, Geoffrey and Trevor. Stewart spent much of his childhood in a poor household in Mirfield, where he experienced domestic violence at the hands of his father, which may have been a result of his wartime PTSD. Stewart said in 2008, "My father was a very potent individual, a very powerful man, who got what he wanted. It was said that when he strode onto the parade ground, birds stopped singing. It was many, many years before I realised how my father inserted himself into my work. I've grown a moustache for Macbeth. My father didn't have one, but when I looked in the mirror just before I went on stage I saw my father's face staring straight back at me."
Stewart attended Crowlees Junior and Infants School, a Church of England–affiliated school in Mirfield. He later attributed his acting career to his English teacher there, Cecil Dormand, who "put a copy of Shakespeare in [Stewart's] hand" and told him to get up and perform. He entered Mirfield Secondary Modern School in 1951, aged 11, and continued to study drama there. Around the same time, he met and befriended fellow actor Brian Blessed during a drama course in Mytholmroyd. At the age of 15, he left school and increased his participation in local theatre. He supported himself by working as a newspaper reporter and obituary writer for a local newspaper, but left after one year when his boss gave him an ultimatum to choose acting or journalism. According to one of his brothers, Stewart would attend theatre rehearsals when he was supposed to be at work and then invent the stories he was reporting or persuade other reporters to cover for him. Stewart gained employment in a furniture store, which allowed him to attend rehearsals with few scheduling conflicts. He found that his thespian talent was applicable to the job, resulting in him becoming a productive salesman while practising his acting technique by tailoring his pitch for each customer. He also trained in boxing. He said that acting served as a means of self-expression in his youth. Stewart and Blessed later received grants to attend the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School. Stewart was the first person who was neither a graduate of Oxford nor Cambridge to receive a grant from West Riding Council.


Career


1959–1986: Early acting roles

Stewart's first professional stage appearance was on 19 May 1959 at the Theatre Royal, Bristol (for the Bristol Old Vic Company), playing Cutpurse (a thief among the audience for the play-within-a-play) in Cyrano de Bergerac, directed by John Hale. Following a period with Manchester's Library Theatre, Stewart became a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966, remaining with them until 1982. He became an associate artist of the company in 1967. He appeared with actors such as Ben Kingsley and Ian Richardson. In January 1967, he made his debut TV appearance on Coronation Street as a fire officer. In 1969, he had a brief TV cameo role as Horatio, opposite Ian Richardson's Hamlet, in a performance of the gravedigger scene as part of episode six of Sir Kenneth Clark's Civilisation television series. During the early 1970s, University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) professor Homer Swander recruited him to help teach US university students about Shakespeare, which led to his breakthrough into Hollywood. He made his Broadway debut as Tom Snout in Peter Brook's 1970 production of A Midsummer Night's Dream, then moved to the Royal National Theatre in the early 1980s. Stewart was a prolific actor in performances by the Royal Shakespeare Company, appearing in more than 60 productions. His first appearance was in 1966 in The Investigation, and in the years that followed he became a core member of the company, taking on three or four major roles each season.
Over the years, Stewart took roles in many major television series without ever becoming a household name. He appeared as Vladimir Lenin in Fall of Eagles; Sejanus in I, Claudius; Karla in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Smiley's People; and Claudius in a 1980 BBC adaptation of Hamlet. He took the romantic male lead in the 1975 BBC adaptation of Elizabeth Gaskell's North and South. He also took the lead, as psychiatric consultant Dr Edward Roebuck, in BBC's Maybury in 1981. He continued to play minor roles in films, such as Ejlert Løvborg in Hedda (1975), King Leondegrance in John Boorman's Excalibur (1981), the character Gurney Halleck in David Lynch's Dune (1984), Dr. Armstrong in Tobe Hooper's Lifeforce (1985), and Henry Grey in Lady Jane (1986), the story of English Queen Lady Jane Grey.
Stewart preferred classical theatre to other genres, asking Doctor Who actress Lalla Ward why she would work in science fiction or on television. In 1987, he nonetheless agreed to work in Hollywood on a revival of Star Trek, after Robert H. Justman saw him while attending a literary reading at UCLA. Stewart knew nothing about the cultural influence of Star Trek or its iconic status in American culture. He was reluctant to sign the standard contract of six years, but did so as he, his agent, and others with whom Stewart consulted all believed the new show would quickly fail, allowing him to return to his London stage career after making some money. Regardless, Stewart's trusted colleague, Ian McKellen, was particularly vocal in advising Stewart not to throw away his theatrical career for this foray into television, which Stewart had to disregard considering the opportunity. While in Hollywood, he spent 18 months using the professional name "Patrick Hewes Stewart" while negotiating the rights to his original name from an American actor who had already registered it with the Screen Actors Guild.


1987–1999: Stardom with Star Trek and Shakespeare

When Stewart was picked for the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation (1987–1994), the Los Angeles Times called him an "unknown British Shakespearean actor". Still living out of his suitcase because of his scepticism that the show would succeed, he was unprepared for the long schedule of television production that began at 4:45 am each day. He initially experienced difficulty fitting in with his less-disciplined castmates. In interviews, he recalled with embarrassment a time when he scolded the main cast for being unprofessional in his opinion, by saying, "We're not here ... to have fun!" Furthermore, Stewart stated that his "spirits used to sink" whenever he was required to memorise and recite technobabble. He eventually came to better understand the cultural differences between the stage and television and relaxed to a degree at work, and his favourite technical phrase became "spacetime continuum". His respect for the genre and work grew to the point that he walked off the set when he discovered that Good Morning America was to film a promotional segment that he saw as belittling the series. He would later write that the role of Picard reminded him of his Shakespearean roles, stating, "I should play Jean-Luc, I realised, as if he were a character in Henry IV, which is about brave men".
Stewart remained close friends with his fellow Star Trek actors and became their advocate with the producers when necessary. Marina Sirtis credited Stewart with "at least 50%, if not more" of the show's success because others imitated his professionalism and dedication to acting. Jonathan Frakes said that, with some shows he had been on, there were actors who showed up without having read the script, but Stewart had "set such a high bar for preparation. We all came to work in the morning completely prepared. We knew our lines and had broken down the script".

Stewart unexpectedly became wealthy because of the show's success. In 1992, during a break in filming, Stewart calculated that he earned more during that break than from ten weeks of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? in London. He also portrayed Picard in Star Trek: Deep Space Nine's 1993 pilot episode "Emissary" and in the films Star Trek Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998), and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002). In 1995, he received a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination for Outstanding Performance by a Male Actor in a Drama Series.
After The Next Generation began, Stewart soon found that he missed acting on the stage. Although he remained associated with the Royal Shakespeare Company, the lengthy filming for the series had prevented him from participating in most other works, leaving a "gaping hole" of many years in his CV as a Shakespearean actor, causing him to miss opportunities to play such notable roles as Hamlet, Romeo, and Richard III. Instead, Stewart began writing one-man shows that he performed in California universities and acting schools. One of these—a version of Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol in which he portrayed all 40-plus characters—became ideal for him as an actor as well, because of its limited performing schedule.
